text: Raylene May Keightley (born 19 November 1961 in Kokstad, former Cape Province) is a South African judge of the Supreme Court of Appeal. She was admitted as an attorney in 1986 and as an advocate in 2006. She matriculated at Umtata High School in Mthatha and earned a BA and LLB from the University of Natal in 1984. Between 1987 and 1988, she completed an LLM at the University of Cambridge, winning the Gonville and Caius College Sir William McNair Prize for the best LLM student. From 1985 to 1986, she was a candidate attorney at Balsillie, Watermeyer and Cawood in Cape Town. Upon returning to South Africa in 1988, she joined the law faculty at the University of Cape Town, teaching as a lecturer until 1995 and then as a senior lecturer from 1991. In 1996, she moved to Johannesburg to become a senior lecturer at the University of the Witwatersrand's School of Law, where she was promoted to professor in 1999 and served as assistant dean that year. Between 1999 and 2001, she was senior state advocate in the Asset Forfeiture Unit of the National Prosecuting Authority. In 2001, she was admitted as an advocate of the High Court of South Africa and was promoted to deputy director of Public Prosecutions in the Asset Forfeiture Unit, before leaving in 2003 to become its regional head in Johannesburg. In July 2006, she left the National Prosecuting Authority to serve her pupillage at the Johannesburg Bar. From 2006 to 2015, she practised law at the Johannesburg Bar, first at the Island Group of Advocates and then at Thulamela Chambers, and served as director of the Centre for Applied Legal Studies at the University of the Witwatersrand from 2008 to 2011. She also served as an acting judge in the Gauteng Division of the High Court for four periods between October 2013 and August 2015. In October 2015, the Judicial Service Commission shortlisted and interviewed her for a permanent vacancy in the Gauteng High Court, recommending her for appointment after interviews, and President Jacob Zuma confirmed her appointment with effect from 1 January 2016. In October 2017, she delivered a landmark ruling declaring corporal punishment by parents unconstitutional, finding that neither religious defences nor the common-law defence of "reasonable chastisement" justified it, a decision upheld by the Constitutional Court in September 2019 in Freedom of Religion South Africa v Minister of Justice and Constitutional Development. Other notable rulings include a July 2019 decision prohibiting the application of set-off to credit agreements under the National Credit Act and an October 2022 ruling reinstating Mpho Phalatse as Mayor of Johannesburg following an unconstitutional vote of no confidence. Keightley served as an acting judge in the Supreme Court of Appeal for two terms between July 2023 and March 2024, during which the court heard an appeal of an Equality Court decision on whether singing 'Dubul' ibhunu’ (“Kill the Boer”) constituted hate speech. AfriForum requested her recusal, citing alleged bias from a 2018 High Court case where Keightley reportedly said AfriForum was “barking up the wrong tree” and suggested counsel might wish to apply for her recusal, but the application was refused. In May 2024, the Judicial Service Commission recommended her for permanent elevation to the Supreme Court of Appeal, which was confirmed by President Cyril Ramaphosa, and she joined the bench on 1 July 2024. She is married to Alan Dodson SC, a prominent advocate and former acting justice of the Constitutional Court, with whom she has three sons.
